\chapter{Review --- The Three Se's}
\label{ch:review-three-se}
\hlchaptermodality{178}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell the three se's apart and say which two are really one word.}

Complete ES-C52-tres-ses: say which two se's are one word and what marks the impostor.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — the three se's}

\label{lesson:ES-C52-tres-ses}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Say \emph{se llama}, then \emph{se habla español}, then \emph{se lo digo}. Three sentences, three \emph{se}s, learned about a hundred chapters apart.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{example} & \textbf{what the \emph{se} is} \\
\midrule
\textbf{reflexive} & \emph{se llama} & himself \\
\textbf{impersonal} & \emph{se habla español} & nobody named \\
\textbf{the impostor} & \emph{se lo digo} & \emph{le}, in disguise \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And here is the fact that makes this a review rather than a fourth thing to learn:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{The first two are the same word. The third is not.}
\end{quote}

The impersonal grew out of the reflexive — \emph{the books sell themselves} becoming \emph{books are sold} — which is why the verb still agrees with the thing. Same word, stretched.

The third only looks like them. It is Latin \emph{illī} — the \emph{le} you already know — which arrived at this spelling by an accident of medieval pronunciation, as you saw when \emph{gelo} became \emph{se lo}.

So Spanish does not have three \emph{se}s. It has \textbf{two, and a coincidence}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: how to tell them apart in the wild}]
You will not have to work this out consciously for long, but while you do:

1. \textbf{Is there a \emph{lo}, \emph{la}, \emph{los} or \emph{las} right after it?} Then it is the impostor: \emph{se lo}, \emph{se la}. It means \emph{to him / to her / to them}. 2. \textbf{Otherwise, is anybody named as the doer?} If not, it is the impersonal: \emph{se habla}, \emph{se dice}, \emph{se come bien}. 3. \textbf{Otherwise it is the reflexive}, pointing back at whoever the sentence is about: \emph{se llama}, \emph{se levanta}.

The first test is nearly free, because that direct object pronoun is sitting right there in the open.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}se llama\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}se habla español\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}se lo digo\textquotedblright{} — two of these are relatives
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many \emph{se}s does Spanish really have? (\textbf{Two, and a coincidence}.) Which one is the impostor? (The one in \emph{\textbf{se lo}} — it is \emph{le}.) Next: all of it in a place you would actually meet it.
\end{tcolorbox}
